R04-D-01: Elections are so closely identified with democracy that it can seem perverse to ask whether they are democratic at all. Yet consider what an election rewards. To win, a candidate must stand out from the crowd: be better known, better funded, better connected or simply more persuasive on a platform than the people whose votes are sought. An election is, in this sense, a procedure for picking a distinguished few, and the chambers it fills tend to resemble the electorate less closely than a random sample of that electorate would. Many ancient Greek writers saw the point clearly; for them, filling offices by lot was the characteristically democratic method, and election was a device that favoured the prominent. The modern case for selection by lot builds on that old intuition. A body drawn at random from the adult population brings into the room the people who are usually spoken about rather than heard: the shift worker, the pensioner, the young parent who would never run for anything. Its members owe nothing to donors or to party managers, since nobody campaigned to put them there. Above all, they are free to change their minds. An elected representative who revises a position after hearing the evidence risks being called a turncoat; a citizen chosen by lot has no platform to betray, and so can treat a question as something to be worked out rather than a position to be defended. Critics usually reply that ordinary citizens lack the competence to legislate. This objection is weaker than it sounds. Few elected legislators are experts in more than a sliver of what they vote on; they rely on staff, committees and witnesses, and there is no reason a randomly chosen body could not do the same. A more serious difficulty concerns accountability. An elected member who disappoints can be removed at the next election, and the prospect of removal disciplines conduct in between. A member chosen by lot answers to no one, and the very independence that shields such a member from donors also shields him or her from voters. Those who propose replacing elected chambers with lotteries have not, to my mind, answered this objection. The sensible conclusion is not that lot should displace election but that it can do something election does badly. On some questions elected politicians have every incentive to avoid committing themselves, because any clear answer will cost them votes. A panel chosen at random, given time, evidence and a duty to hear opposing witnesses, can show what ordinary people conclude once they have actually thought the matter through, and its recommendations can then be put to the legislature or to the voters for decision. The lottery's virtue is that it reveals considered public judgement; its limit is that no one has authorised the people it selects to rule.
R04-D-02: In a handful of democracies, adults who fail to vote without a good excuse are fined a small sum. To many people elsewhere this looks like a contradiction in terms: surely a free citizen is entitled to stay at home. The objection deserves a hearing, but it is less forceful than it first appears. What such laws typically require is attendance, not a vote for anyone in particular. Ballots remain secret, and a citizen who wishes to register indifference or protest can spoil the ballot paper or leave it blank. The duty imposed is closer to that of serving on a jury or completing a census form than to an order about what to believe. A subtler version of the objection holds that deliberate abstention is itself a political statement, a refusal to lend legitimacy to a contest one regards as empty. Yet a citizen who feels this way loses very little under compulsion, since the blank ballot preserves the statement and arguably sharpens it: a deliberately empty ballot can be counted, whereas a deliberate absence is indistinguishable from the absences of those who merely forgot. The more interesting question is what compulsion actually changes. Where voting is voluntary, turnout is usually lowest among the young, the poor and the recently arrived, so the electorate that politicians court is older and wealthier than the population as a whole. Campaigns respond rationally to this. A large share of their effort goes into persuading their own likely supporters to turn up, and one of the cheapest ways to do that is to make those supporters angry or afraid about the other side. When almost everyone votes, that strategy loses much of its point. There is little to be gained by stirring up people who will vote anyway, and the votes worth competing for belong to citizens who have not yet made up their minds. Supporters of compulsion sometimes go further and claim that it produces wiser decisions. Here caution is needed. Being required to attend a polling station does not make anyone better informed, and a citizen who resents the obligation may simply mark the first name on the list. Compulsion enlarges the electorate; it does not educate it. Its real contribution is quieter. It shifts the incentives of those who seek votes, away from rousing the faithful and towards addressing the undecided, and it allows the result to claim to speak for nearly everyone rather than for those who happened to feel strongly enough to come out. That is a modest achievement, but in an age of angry campaigning it is not a small one.
R04-D-03: The secret ballot is now so taken for granted that it is easy to forget how recent it is and how fiercely it was once opposed. For much of the nineteenth century, in many countries, voters declared their choices aloud or on papers that others could see, and the reform that replaced this practice was resisted not only by those who profited from intimidation. A respectable strand of liberal opinion held that the vote was a public trust, exercised on behalf of the whole community, and that a trust ought to be discharged in public. A man who knew that his neighbours would see his vote, the argument ran, would be ashamed to cast it for a selfish reason. The argument has a certain nobility, and it rests on a real insight: people do behave differently when they are observed. Its error lies in assuming that the observer will be the voter's conscience. In practice the people most interested in how a tenant, a labourer or a clerk had voted were the landlord, the employer and the local party agent, and the pressure they applied had little to do with the public good. Publicity did not make votes more responsible; it made them more obedient. The less obvious virtue of secrecy is that it disarms bribery as well as intimidation. Buying a vote is a kind of contract, and a contract is worthless if one party cannot check whether the other has kept it. Once no one can verify how a ballot was marked, the buyer who pays in advance cannot know whether he has bought anything, and the seller can take the money and vote as he pleases. Secrecy, in other words, works less by appealing to the voter's virtue than by making a certain kind of corruption unenforceable. This also explains why secrecy has to be a duty and not merely a right. If voters could choose to reveal their ballots, those under pressure could be required to prove their compliance, and the protection would collapse for exactly the people who need it most. That point matters more now than it once did. A ballot marked at home, at a kitchen table, can be watched by a domineering relative; a ballot photographed in a booth with a telephone can be shown to whoever demands proof. Neither practice is sinister in itself, and both make voting easier for many people. But they reopen the gap that secrecy was designed to close, and they suggest that the privacy of the vote is not a natural condition of democratic life but an arrangement that has to be maintained, and occasionally rebuilt, as the means of voting change.
R04-D-04: Few political terms are used as loosely as populism. It is applied to movements of the left and of the right, to leaders who promise to spend lavishly and to those who promise to cut, to campaigns against banks and to campaigns against immigrants. A word that covers so much risks covering nothing, and some scholars have concluded that it is merely a label for whatever kind of politics the speaker happens to dislike. That conclusion is premature. The variety of populist programmes is real, but it may simply show that populism is not a programme at all. Consider the most common attempt at definition: populism as hostility to elites. This cannot be sufficient, since criticism of the powerful is the ordinary business of opposition in any democracy, and a definition that made every challenger a populist would be useless. What distinguishes the populist is a further claim, namely that there exists a single, authentic people whose will is already known, and that the movement or leader in question alone gives it voice. Opponents are therefore not merely mistaken; they are illegitimate, and citizens who vote for them are not quite part of the people. On this account the core of populism is not anti-elitism but anti-pluralism, a refusal to accept that the people may be divided in good faith. The value of this definition is that it explains a pattern which approaches based on policy tend to miss. A movement that claims to embody the whole people has difficulty accepting defeat, since a loss at the polls must then be explained as fraud, manipulation or the work of enemies; and once in office it is tempted to treat independent courts, a critical press or a neutral civil service as obstacles placed between the people and its rightful expression. None of this follows from hostility to elites alone. It follows from the claim to a moral monopoly of representation. Yet the definition carries a hazard of its own. Precisely because it locates the danger in a style of claim rather than in a set of grievances, it can tempt those who use it to dismiss the grievances along with the style. Many people drawn to populist movements have real complaints: about decisions taken far away from them, about parties that seem interchangeable, about institutions that consult them rarely. To treat such voters as a symptom to be managed, rather than as citizens with reasons, is to deny them the standing that pluralism promises, and to confirm the populist story that an elite has stopped listening. The definition is a tool for recognising a threat to democratic competition; it is not a licence to stop asking why the threat finds an audience.
R04-D-05: Political parties have few admirers. It is a commonplace of political commentary that they are distrusted, and reformers of every persuasion have proposed ways of loosening their grip: independent candidates, direct votes on policy, primaries open to any voter who cares to take part. The suspicion is understandable. Parties reward loyalty over judgement, they paper over disagreements in order to win, and their leaders sometimes seem more interested in the survival of the organisation than in the purposes it was founded to serve. Yet much of what makes democratic government workable is done by parties, and done so routinely that it goes unnoticed. A modern electorate contains millions of people with conflicting interests. Someone has to assemble those interests into a programme coherent enough to be offered, defended and, if elected, attempted; someone has to recruit and test the people who will hold office; and someone has to give voters a simple way of knowing what a candidate broadly stands for without studying the record of each individual. Parties do all three. Most importantly, they make accountability possible. A government formed by a party can be judged as a team at the next election, whereas a legislature of independents, each with a private bargain to defend, offers voters no one in particular to reward or punish. This is why some reforms intended to democratise parties have had awkward consequences. When candidates are chosen in primaries open to anyone, the party organisation loses much of its ability to screen out those who would damage it, and the candidates who win are often those with the most intense supporters rather than those with the broadest appeal. When membership dwindles, the organisation does not disappear; it becomes a smaller circle of professionals and funders, less rooted in local life and more remote from the voters it claims to represent. Weakening the party, in other words, does not necessarily hand power to citizens. It may hand it instead to whoever is able to organise without one: wealthy individuals, single-issue lobbies, the personal following of a celebrity. None of this makes parties virtuous. A party that faces no serious competition will serve itself, and the defenders of party government have sometimes mistaken the indispensability of parties for their innocence. The argument here is a narrower one. It is that the familiar complaints about parties are complaints about particular parties behaving badly, and that the cure for bad parties is better ones, more open to their members and more seriously contested, rather than a politics that tries to do without them altogether.
R04-D-06: A common complaint about protest is that it inconveniences people who have done nothing wrong. Commuters are delayed, shops lose trade, ambulances must find another route. The complaint has some force, but it often hides an assumption that deserves to be questioned: that legitimate protest would cause no inconvenience at all. A march that nobody notices, held where nobody has to walk around it, is hardly a protest. Part of the point of gathering in public is to make a claim that others cannot easily ignore. This is why disruption has always been close to the centre of democratic protest rather than at its edge. Groups without money, office or access to the press have few ways of placing an issue on the public agenda, and a temporary cost imposed on the wider community is one of them. Many causes now regarded as plainly just were first brought to public notice by people who were considered a nuisance, and their critics complained, in much the same terms as are heard today, that they had chosen the wrong methods and the wrong moment. None of this means that any disruption is acceptable. The useful distinction is between disruption that seeks a hearing and disruption that seeks to impose an outcome. The first imposes a cost in order to make others pay attention; it accepts that, once they have paid attention, they may still disagree. The second tries to make it impossible for others to act on their own decision, for instance by preventing a lawful vote from taking place or by keeping people from a service they are entitled to use. Protest of the first kind is part of the argument on which democracy runs. Protest of the second kind substitutes pressure for persuasion, and a democracy can rightly limit it. Proportion matters as well. A blockade that delays traffic for an afternoon is different from one that prevents a hospital from receiving supplies, even if both are aimed only at securing attention. Those who protest have a responsibility to choose methods whose costs bear some relation to the importance of what they are saying, and those who govern have a responsibility not to treat every inconvenience as an emergency. Neither responsibility can be reduced to a simple rule, and particular cases will always be argued over; but the alternative to such argument is worse. A society that tolerates no disruption at all has, in effect, decided that only those who already have a hearing deserve one.
R04-D-07: When a town loses its newspaper, the loss is usually mourned in the language of community: the obituaries, the school sports results, the notices of births and marriages that no one else will print. These are real losses, but they are not the ones that matter most for self-government. What disappears with the local paper is something duller and more important, namely the habit of attendance. For decades, in many places, a reporter sat through the meetings of the council, the planning committee and the school board, read the budget documents that nobody else read, and noticed when a contract went to the same firm for the third time without a tender. Most of what such reporters wrote was unremarkable, and much of it was barely read. Its value lay less in any particular story than in the knowledge, shared by every official in the room, that someone was taking notes. Officials who know that a question may be asked in print tomorrow tend to ask it of themselves today. Monitoring of this kind works rather as a speed camera does: its effect is measured not by the fines it issues but by the careless driving it prevents. Remove it, and the immediate result is not a wave of scandal, since there is no longer anyone to report one, but a gradual loosening of the restraint that observation imposed. The absence of bad news, in a town without a reporter, is not evidence of good government. It is often said that the internet has more than made up the difference, since anyone can now publish and residents can share information instantly. This confuses the supply of commentary with the supply of attention. A neighbourhood forum can spread a rumour about the council in minutes, but it seldom has anyone willing to spend three evenings a month in council meetings, or the training to read a set of accounts. National outlets, for their part, cover local government only when it produces a story large enough to interest a national audience, which is usually to say only after the damage is done. What the internet has multiplied is reaction; what has thinned out is the patient, unglamorous observation on which informed reaction depends. None of this should be allowed to turn into nostalgia. Many local papers were timid with powerful advertisers, cosy with the town's leading figures and given to boosterism, celebrating every new development while asking few questions about who would profit from it. A press that depends on the goodwill of the people it covers is a weak watchdog, and some of the papers now lamented were weak in exactly this way, flattering the very people they ought to have been questioning. The case for local journalism does not rest on the virtue of the institutions that happened to provide it. It rests, rather, on the function those institutions performed, however imperfectly. If that function is to survive the collapse of the business model that once paid for it, it will have to be supported deliberately: by newsrooms funded as public goods, by universities that send students to cover meetings, perhaps by public records published in forms that a busy citizen can actually read. Each of these options carries hazards, and money from the very governments that journalists are meant to watch carries the most obvious one. But a democracy that leaves the observation of its local governments to chance should not be surprised when those governments begin to behave as if no one is looking.
R04-D-08: That most citizens know little about the policies they vote on is one of the most frequently confirmed observations about modern democracies, and one of the least surprising. A single vote almost never decides an election, and the hours needed to master the details of tax law or trade policy are hours taken from work, family and sleep. Ignorance, in these circumstances, is not a failure of character. It is what a sensible person would choose if he or she treated the vote as a decision with private costs and a vanishingly small chance of making a difference. Economists call this rational ignorance, and the label is apt: the problem is not that voters reason badly but that they have little reason to acquire what good reasoning would need. Two very different conclusions are drawn from this. The first, which has gained a certain academic following, is that the franchise should be weighted towards those who know more, since a decision made by the informed is likely to be better than one made by everyone. The second, more common among defenders of democracy, is that ignorance matters less than it seems, because voters rely on shortcuts. They need not study a programme if they know which party proposed it; they need not understand monetary policy to notice whether prices are rising; they can follow the advice of an organisation they trust. A voter equipped with such cues, the argument goes, can vote much as she would if she were fully informed. The second conclusion is more attractive than the first, but it claims too much. A shortcut is only as good as the connection between the cue and the thing the voter actually cares about, and that connection is not guaranteed. Party labels are informative when parties are stable and their programmes distinct; when parties fragment or converge, the label says little. Judging a government by how things are going is reasonable if the government controls how things are going, but voters who punish an incumbent for a drought, or for a downturn that began abroad, are using a cue that measures luck as much as competence. And an endorsement is valuable only if the endorser shares the voter's interests, which is precisely what a well-funded campaign may try to disguise. Shortcuts, in short, do not make ignorance harmless; they make its effects depend on the environment in which voters find themselves. That dependence, however, is also the strongest reply to those who would ration the vote. If the quality of popular judgement varies with the reliability of the cues available, then the natural remedy is to improve the cues rather than to disqualify the people who use them. Parties with clear and lasting identities, intermediaries whose interests are visible, a press that reports what governments actually control: each of these makes ordinary shortcuts more trustworthy. Weighting votes by knowledge, by contrast, would leave the environment of cues untouched while inviting a quarrel, unlikely ever to be settled impartially, about who should set the test and what it should contain. Neither side, then, has quite grasped the problem. The critics are right that an uninformed electorate can be misled, and the defenders are right that citizens need not be experts to judge well. What both overlook is that the competence of voters is not a fixed property of individuals but partly a product of institutions, and that a democracy can therefore make its citizens wiser as voters without making any of them more learned.
